claims.text: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by a temperature-dependent short-range-order transition.
The critical transition temperature in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is approximately 600 °C.
Crossing below the critical temperature triggers nucleation of partially ordered B2 from a disordered BCC state.
The initial high-temperature state of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is a disordered BCC solid solution.
Annealing below approximately 600 °C enables substantial evolution of short-range order.
Temperature-induced short-range order mediates the nucleation and growth of B2 clusters within a disordered BCC matrix.
An interplay between composition-dependent thermodynamic instability and kinetic activation of short-range order drives a sharp ordering transition.
Below the critical temperature, the free-energy benefit of ordering becomes sufficient to overcome kinetic barriers.
Samples annealed below approximately 600 °C will have a larger B2 phase fraction than samples maintained at higher temperatures.
Samples annealed below approximately 600 °C will exhibit stronger short-range-order signatures.
The ordering transformation may enhance yield strength.
Slow cooling is required to allow the proposed short-range-order-mediated B2 transformation.
Rapid quenching will kinetically suppress B2 formation.
The high-temperature baseline is homogeneous disordered BCC with minimal short-range order.
Integrated simulations and thermodynamic predictions support a critical temperature near 600 °C for the target alloy.
Homogenization at 800 °C will ensure a uniform disordered BCC starting state in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
X-ray diffraction can quantify BCC and B2 phase fractions in the treated samples.
Transmission electron microscopy can resolve short-range order and B2 cluster formation.
Differential scanning calorimetry can detect thermal events associated with ordering.
Failure to observe increased B2 fraction or short-range-order evolution at or below approximately 600 °C relative to the high-temperature control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The proposed high-temperature comparator is annealed at 650 °C but then slow-cooled, so it will traverse the hypothesized sub-600 °C transformation regime. It therefore is not actually maintained above the critical temperature and may not provide the intended high-temperature control.
